newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss shares seen ekeing out further 1997 gains.
newsitem.headline: Swiss shares seen ekeing out further 1997 gains.

text.p: Swiss shares should still eke out further gains this year, but the market is vulnerable and likely to take a few dips during the year on interest rate and currency worries, analysts and market strategists said.
Despite such brief scares, most analysts remain bullish for Swiss shares based on strong corporate earnings and a sluggish economy that will keep interest rates in check.
"The climate at present is much more favourable for a continuation of the bull market," Bank Julius Baer's research team wrote in its latest Market View.
Like most other "exuberant" equity markets, the Swiss stock market got off to a roaring start in 1997 with share prices quickly exceeding all previous forecasts and price targets.

By mid-February Swiss stocks had risen some 14 percent as foreign investors joined the bull run that was triggered by lower interest rates and a decline in the Swiss franc, which makes Swiss products more competitive and thus boosts earnings.

Analysts consequently raised targets by an average 15 percent and nine Swiss analysts now on average expect the blue-chip Swiss Market Index (SMI) to reach 4,770 points by year-end, a gain of 4.0 percent from its close on Tuesday.
The broad Swiss Performance Index (SPI) is forecast to end 1997 at 3,054 points, up 6.4 percent from Tuesday.
The latest forecasts imply an expected gain of 21 percent in the SMI in 1997 compared with a rise of 19.5 percent in 1996.

The forecasts, obtained during a Reuters poll on March 12, compare with forecasts from December 1996, which on average called for the SMI to rise to 4,155 points by the end of 1997 and the SPI to hit 2,676 points.

Despite the favourable fundamentals, the rally in the first quarter has unnerved some analysts, who see investors becoming unsettled by the almost-daily reports of new records that have awakened memories of Black Monday in 1987.
"The market should peak in the next couple of months," said Pierre Tissot of Lombard Odier et Cie.
After a rapid surge in the first six weeks of 1997, Swiss shares entered a healthy two-week consolidation phase in late February, taking some of the froth out of the market.
As if to underscore that corporate earnings growth is strong, but not without limits, blue chips ABB Asea Brown Boveri AG and watchmaker SMH reported less-than spectacular results.
But since early March the bulls are back.
"At this level the market is no longer cheap and corrections can't be excluded," added Hans-Peter Ast, head of broker research at Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS).
Many analysts expect a correction during the second or third quarter, triggered by an increase in U.S. interest rates or a correction in the dollar's strength that hits U.S. markets.
"At some point over the next six months I expect a dollar scare," said Frederick Hasslauer of Sal. Oppenheim.
A fall in U.S. markets is widely expected to infect European markets, but only briefly.
Investors' confidence in European and Swiss stocks is expected to return quickly as favourable exchange rates and low interest rates herald continued earnings growth.

"There are few other alternatives to shares," added Christoph Streit at Bank Leu, noting that pension funds are also turning their backs on property as an investment in favour of shares, another reason that liquidity in equity markets is high.
"Investors are willing to accept a lower risk premium because there are no alternatives," added Josef Scherer of Credit Suisse First Boston (CSFB).

Swiss shares should weather any draft from U.S. markets better than most European markets because the Swiss economy is lagging the German economy, which is expected to gradually pull out of the doldrums during the second half of 1997.
"Even if the Bundesbank were to raise interest rates in the second half of 1997, the Swiss National Bank might not follow because the economy is lagging and in bad shape," Tissot said.
-- Zurich Editorial +41 1 631 7340
